note: Data-size reference points for the quiz. Values match the Logcaliper iOS app's comparison catalogue (AppDelegate.m, pickedBytesSize); where the app once disagreed with itself — an Internet Archive sized at 700 PB under a description reading 70 PB, a gram of DNA computing with 230.69 PB against a stated 215 PB, a Library of Congress figure that was the printed text rather than the digital archive, a Spotify row labelled Normal Quality at the High Quality bitrate — both sides have been corrected together and now agree. The seven pure units (Bytes, Kilobytes ... Exabytes) are left out, since 'is a terabyte bigger than a gigabyte' teaches nothing. Labels avoid naming their own size: the app's names for CD-ROM, DVD and Blu-Ray contain theirs, which would give the answer away.

units.label: A page of text
units.note: About 2,000 characters.

units.label: A 500-page eBook
units.note: Plain text, simple formatting.

units.label: A high-resolution photo
units.note: A typical 5 MB JPEG.

units.label: One ProRAW photo
units.note: Apple's raw format, around 25 MB a frame.

units.label: An hour of Spotify
units.note: At high quality. Normal quality is roughly half that.
units.reconciled: 72 MB/hour is 160 kbps, Spotify's High setting; the app used to label it Normal Quality and now says High.

units.label: A CD-ROM
units.note: 80 minutes of audio.

units.label: An hour of Netflix in HD
units.note: Roughly 3 GB an hour.

units.label: A DVD
units.note: One feature film.

units.label: An hour of YouTube in 4K
units.note: Nearly twice an hour of HD Netflix.

units.label: English Wikipedia's article text
units.note: Every article, compressed, without media or revision history. Smaller than most people expect.

units.label: A Blu-Ray disc
units.note: One high-definition film.

units.label: Fortnite on PC
units.note: The install alone is bigger than English Wikipedia's text.

units.label: A large open-weights AI model
units.note: Tens of billions of parameters, about 45 GB on disk. Frontier models are far larger.

units.label: A day of James Webb data
units.note: What the space telescope sends home daily.

units.label: An hour of ProRes video
units.note: The editing format, not the delivery one.

units.label: An iPhone's storage
units.note: A mid-range handset.

units.label: A typical cloud drive
units.note: What a consumer plan gives you.

units.label: A PlayStation 5's drive
units.note: One terabyte.

units.label: The text of the Library of Congress
units.note: Just the words of the print collection. The Library's actual digital archive is over a thousand times larger.
units.reconciled: 15 TB is the old estimate for the printed collection's text, not the digital archive; the app's description now says so.

units.label: A human brain
units.note: An estimate of its storage equivalent.

units.label: A day at one social network
units.note: What a single large platform generates daily — logs and telemetry included, not just posts.

units.label: Google Earth
units.note: The whole imagery database.

units.label: The Internet Archive
units.note: Roughly 99 PB of unique data — texts, audio, video and software, not only the Wayback Machine.
units.reconciled: the app used to size this at 700 PB under a description reading 70 PB; both now say the ~99 PB the Archive publishes.

units.label: One gram of DNA
units.note: Theoretical storage density. More than twice everything the Internet Archive holds.
units.reconciled: the app computed with 230.69 PB against its own stated 215 PB; both now use the published 215 PB.
